newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Australian to be named UN Iraqi disarmament chief.
newsitem.headline: Australian to be named UN Iraqi disarmament chief.

text.p: Australia's U.N. ambassador, Richard Butler, was expected to be named officially on Thursday as executive chairman of the U.N. commission in charge of Iraqi disarmament, diplomats said.

He will replace Rolf Ekeus of Sweden, who has led the U.N. Special Commission, known as UNSCOM, since its inception in 1991. Ekeus expects to leave in July to become Sweden's ambassador to Washington.

The choice of a successor to Ekeus was up to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan. Diplomats said he consulted informally with the five permanent Security Council members -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China. Ekeus was said to have recommended Butler.

UNSCOM is in charge of eliminating Iraq's weapons of mass destruction. The oil embargo and other sanctions against Iraq, imposed after it invaded Kuwait in 1990, cannot be lifted until the commission is satisfied it has accounted for all its biological, chemical and ballistic arms.

Butler, 54, known for his articulate and blunt comments, has been involved in disarmament affairs since 1983, when he was appointed Australia's first ambassador at the Geneva-based Conference on Disarmament for five years.
Ekeus held the same post for Sweden and the two men became acquainted at that time, diplomats said.
Butler made world headlines in 1995 when he successfully pushed a General Assembly resolution aimed at denouncing nuclear tests by France and China.
A year later he moved quickly to save the nuclear test ban treaty by getting the General Assembly to open it for signature after Geneva arms negotiations failed because of opposition from India.
Butler came to the United Nations in 1992 after serving as ambassador in Thailand as well as his country's representative in Cambodia.

He was selected shortly afterwards to several posts by his colleagues. In 1992 he was elected chairman of the committee organising the world body's 1995 50th anniversary celebrations. In 1994 he was elected president of the U.N. Economic and Social Council and was chosen vice chairman of the summit on poverty held in Copenhagen in March 1955.

In 1995 Butler convened the Canberra Commission on the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, which produced a landmark report. The commission included former U.S. Defence Secretary Robert McNamara as well as Ekeus.

But despite the fact he was sought out repeatedly to head difficult U.N. projects, he lost his country's bid for a non-permanent seat on the 15-member Security Council late last year. The assembly instead voted for Portugal.
The U.N. Special Commission, on instructions from the Security Council, was organised by Ekeus in April 1991. It is considered one of the most efficient bodies in the United Nations.
Ekeus has frequently accused Iraq of misleading his weapons inspectors, and in turn has been accused by Baghdad officials of doing Washington's bidding.
